# ANOVA Example (By Hand)

In an attempt to explain the handwritten operations on slide 12, we repeat the same operations here in R. To begin with, let us write down our data:

```{r}
N <- 10
a <- c(100, 134, 132, 125, 121, 144, 110, 133, 113, 145)
b <- c(120, 154, 152, 150, 141, 161, 131, 160, 132, 154)
c <- c(130, 160, 161, 157, 151, 170, 140, 165, 142, 162)
```

Next, we compute the corresponding means (for each hospital and the global mean):

```{r}
ma <- mean(a)
mb <- mean(b)
mc <- mean(c)
m <- mean(c(a, b, c))
```

We now proceed to compute SSW:

```{r}
sswa <- sum((a - ma)^2)
sswb <- sum((b - mb)^2)
sswc <- sum((c - mc)^2)
ssw <- sswa + sswb + sswc
```

Now, we also need to compute SSB:

```{r}
ms <- c(ma, mb, mc)
ssb <- 10 * sum((ms - m)^2)
```

At last, we compute the corresponding F statistic:

```{r}
k <- 3 # Number of samples
df_enum <- k - 1
df_denom <- 3*N - k
f_stat <- (ssb / df_enum) / (ssw / df_denom)
print(f_stat)
```
Now, what remains is to actually find the probability with which we get this F-stat
value:

```{r}
# pf() returns the cutoff point for the rightmost tail for the F distribution.
p <- 1 - pf(f_stat, df_enum, df_denom)
print(p)
```
So, the computed p value in our case is $p=0.0003297989$.


# ANOVA Example (By R)

We first create three columns for our data:

```{r}
a <- c(100, 134, 132, 125, 121, 144, 110, 133, 113, 145)
b <- c(120, 154, 152, 150, 141, 161, 131, 160, 132, 154)
c <- c(130, 160, 161, 157, 151, 170, 140, 165, 142, 162)
```

Now, we can combine those as in the slides into a single table:

```{r}
hospital_stay <- data.frame(c(a, b, c), c(rep('A', 10), rep('B', 10), rep('C', 10)))
print(hospital_stay)
```
Also, we change colnames:

```{r}
names(hospital_stay) <- c('StayDuration', 'Hospital')
```

We can now perform an ANOVA as simply as:

```{r}
oneway.test(hospital_stay$StayDuration ~ hospital_stay$Hospital)
```

The results imply that we have actually a good reason to reject the null hypothesis, i.e., stay duration across all three hospitals is not the same.

We can also get the same results (by default, assuming equal variances) using Bartlett's test:

```{r}
bartlett.test(hospital_stay$StayDuration ~ hospital_stay$Hospital)
```


> Observe that when running ANOVA by hand, we got a p value of 0.0003, while `oneway.test()` yielded a p value around 0.001. This is due to the default assumption of oneway.test() that variances are not the same. If we want, we can demand that this assumption is true, as follows:

```{r}
oneway.test(hospital_stay$StayDuration ~ hospital_stay$Hospital, var.equal = TRUE)
```
